title: HCI — Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules (story explainer)
description: Exam revision told as a story: all eight golden rules of interface design with the examples from the notes (Amazon, Canva, Google Drive, Outlook, YouTube, Capian).
endCard: 📘 Eight Golden Rules — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: Why some apps feel effortless — and others make you want to throw your phone

lines: Have you ever used an app that just felt right? And another that made you want to throw your phone?
The difference usually comes down to eight simple rules.
Let's follow Riya on a shopping trip, and watch each golden rule save her day.

scenes.title: 1. Who is Ben Shneiderman?

items.b: American scientist, expert in human–machine interaction; many of his works are fundamental today — e.g. he created the Treemap
principles from his experience — refined, developed and explained — applicable to interactive systems
eight heuristics that help designers solve problems and make interfaces user-friendly

lines: First, who made these rules? Ben Shneiderman, an American scientist and expert in human machine interaction. Many of his works are fundamental today, like the Treemap.
From his experience, he proposed eight principles. After being refined and explained, they apply to any interactive system.
They're eight heuristics, rules of thumb, that help designers solve problems. Because to improve usability, an interface must be well designed, and user friendly.

scenes.title: 2. All eight at a glance

viz.note: “Cats Seldom Fetch Cold Eggs, Rather Lick Milk”

lines: Here are all eight.
Consistency. Shortcuts. Feedback. Closure. Errors. Reversal. Locus of control. Memory.
That's C, S, F, C, E, R, L, M.
Memory hook: Cats Seldom Fetch Cold Eggs, Rather Lick Milk.

scenes.title: Rule 1 — Strive for consistency

items.b: Riya browses Amazon: home page, product page, cart. The Add to Cart button is always the same shape, size and colour. She never hunts for it.
layout · button size · colour code · tone of writing — across the whole site
builds your identity and stops users getting lost as they navigate

lines: Rule one: strive for consistency. Riya browses Amazon. Home page, product page, cart page. The layout is the same, the buttons are always similar in size, and the colours are unmistakably Amazon.
Whether it's the layout, the button size, the colour code, or the tone of writing, keep it consistent across the whole site.
Consistency builds your identity, and users won't get lost as they navigate.

scenes.title: Rule 2 — Enable frequent users to use shortcuts

items.b: Riya designs a poster in Canva. As a beginner she used menus; now she presses Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V and flies.
reach every part of the site in a minimum of clicks — good menu hierarchy, clear labels
features for both: keyboard shortcuts, macro facilities

lines: Rule two: enable frequent users to use shortcuts. Riya designs a poster in Canva. At first she used menus. Now she presses control C and control V, and she flies.
Let users reach every part of the site in a minimum of clicks, with a good menu hierarchy and clear labels.
Include features for both beginners and advanced users, like keyboard shortcuts or macro facilities.

scenes.title: Rule 3 — Offer informative feedback

items.b: Riya drags a video into a Google Drive folder. A window pops up: Uploading 1 item… 45%. She knows it's working.
when users act, show feedback immediately so they know where their process is
users wonder: did it work? Should I click again?

lines: Rule three: offer informative feedback. Riya creates a folder in Google Drive and drags a video into it. Instantly a little window appears: uploading, forty five percent.
Whenever users perform an action, show feedback immediately, so they know where their process stands.
Without it, Riya would wonder: did it work? Should I drag it again?

scenes.title: Rule 4 — Design dialogs to yield closure

viz.note: Closure reduces mental load — the user sees the path of the action end

lines: Rule four: design dialogs to yield closure. Riya's purchase has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
At the end, the site shows a summary, then: order placed, thank you! A thank you message, a validation message, a summary during a purchase.
Close every interaction clearly. When users see their action reach its end, their mental load drops and the experience improves.

scenes.title: Rule 5 — Offer simple error handling

items.b: Riya mistypes her password. The site says: “Incorrect password. Forgot password?” — clear, with a fix.
design to avoid errors as much as possible
if something goes wrong: clear error notifications + descriptive hints to resolve it

lines: Rule five: offer simple error handling. Riya logs in and mistypes her password. The site clearly says the login details are wrong, and offers a fix.
A good interface is designed to avoid errors as much as possible.
But when something does go wrong, make it easy to understand and resolve, with clear error notifications and descriptive hints.

scenes.title: Rule 6 — Permit easy reversal of actions

items.b: In the Outlook app, Riya archives the wrong email. A bar pops up at the bottom: “Archived · Undo”. Phew.
knowing there's an easy way back → users feel less anxious
they become willing to explore options · applies to single actions or groups of actions

lines: Rule six: permit easy reversal of actions. In the Outlook mobile app, Riya archives the wrong email. A small window appears at the bottom, offering to undo. Phew.
Discovering that cancel is easy after a mistake is a great feeling. Users become less anxious,
and more willing to explore. Reversal can apply to single operations or whole groups of operations.

scenes.title: Rule 7 — Support internal locus of control

items.b: On Capian's YouTube page, Riya chooses the bell setting: All · Personalised · None. She decides.
users should feel they are in control of the system
some form of free will reassures the user

lines: Rule seven: support an internal locus of control. On Capian's YouTube page, Riya decides whether to turn on notifications, and how many she wants.
Give users control and freedom, so they feel they are running the system, not the other way round.
That free will reassures them. YouTube makes users feel in control of what they receive.

scenes.title: Rule 8 — Reduce short-term memory load

items.b: Capian's home page is minimalist: one clear call-to-action, nothing to distract Riya
human short-term memory is limited
keep displays simple · consolidate multi-page displays · reduce window-motion frequency · allow training time for codes, mnemonics & action sequences
don't overload with same-level info; decide what goes first — home page or menus

lines: Rule eight: reduce short term memory load. Human short term memory is limited.
So keep displays simple, consolidate multiple page displays, reduce how often windows move, and allow enough training time for codes, mnemonics and sequences of actions.
Don't overload a page with information of the same level. Decide what goes first, whether on the home page or in menus, or you'll lose the user's attention.
Capian's home page is minimalist. Riya's attention goes straight to the call to action, with nothing to distract her.

scenes.title: 3. Conclusion

items.b: the rules are not to be followed blindly
they orient your audits of an interface
detect the main issues in your web interfaces

lines: To conclude: Shneiderman's rules are not gospel.
But clear guidelines orient your interface audits, and help you detect the main problems in your web interfaces.

scenes.title: Recap

viz.s: Cats Seldom Fetch Cold Eggs, Rather Lick Milk

lines: Recap with Riya's trip.
Amazon stays consistent. Canva gives shortcuts. Google Drive gives feedback. The checkout gives closure.
The login explains errors. Outlook lets her undo. YouTube puts her in control. And Capian keeps it simple for her memory. You've got this.
